# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains most of the engineering behind a municipal water system. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62.4 pounds, and a column of water only one inch square but ten feet tall already exerts over four pounds of pressure at its base. Every design decision in a city's water infrastructure—from where reservoirs sit to why your shower weakens at dinner time—flows from this relationship between elevation, weight, and pressure.

## The Fundamental Principle: Gravity Does the First Shift

Imagine a city we'll call Riverton. Its main reservoir sits in hills three miles from downtown, at an elevation of 400 feet above sea level. The tallest apartment building downtown, the Meridian Tower, rises twenty stories, with its top-floor fixtures at roughly 220 feet elevation. The key insight is that water in an open reservoir, connected by a full pipe, will seek its own level. If the pipe network is full and unobstructed, the reservoir's water surface "pushes" water through the system with a pressure determined entirely by the vertical distance between the reservoir surface and the point of use.
